summary: Fourteen days of Nightscout data show good CGM coverage (98.7%) with an average glucose of 121.6 mg/dL, time-in-range 86.0%, time-above-range 8.9%, and time-below-range 5.1%, alongside distinct hypoglycemia clusters (08-13, 08-14, 08-21) and hyperglycemia clusters (08-15, 08-18). A recurring daytime rise peaking around local hour 16 (average 162.8 mg/dL, 32.1% time above range) coincides with the lowest scheduled basal segment (0.5 U/h at 16:00), while repeated correction boluses are frequently followed by large glucose falls 120-360 minutes later, consistent with insulin-on-board stacking against a 10-hour DIA. No carbohydrate entries exist anywhere in the 14-day period, which blocks carb-ratio and e-carb assessment and confines all meal-related glucose management to reactive SMB/UAM correction dosing. Autosens is disabled in favor of Dynamic ISF, which shows wide effective-sensitivity swings that may partly compensate for a single flat ISF segment rather than reflecting an automation defect. The profile is treated as authoritative for the full period per user declaration, though an internal profile-switch event on 08-13 introduces residual timeline uncertainty that lowers confidence in some inferences involving the first week.

analysis_steps.findings: CGM coverage is strong (98.7%, 5-minute cadence, 10 gaps, largest 65 minutes, 0 invalid/duplicate entries). Zero carbohydrate entries exist for the entire period. A Profile Switch event on 2026-08-13 referencing a basal total matching the current profile creates timeline uncertainty for the first six days, but profile_context declares historical_applicability as yes, which is treated as authoritative per package instructions; this is now used, and earlier limited-applicability speculation is corrected downward to a residual uncertainty note only. Only samples of treatments and device statuses are included, though full-period aggregates (treatment_summary, daily_glucose) are trustworthy.

analysis_steps.findings: Aggregate CV is 32.6% and TBR 5.1% exceeds typical guidance. Level-2 hypoglycemia clusters occurred on 2026-08-13, 08-14, and 08-21; severe hyperglycemia clusters occurred on 08-15 and 08-18. Multiple correction-to-later-drop patterns in therapy_response_windows suggest IOB stacking interacting with the 10-hour DIA. Dynamic ISF effective sensitivity ranges roughly from 27.8 to 178.7 mg/dL/U across loop snapshots. A pump occlusion/error was logged on 08-19 and GLP-1 doses were logged on 08-14, 08-17, and 08-20, both plausible confounders for isolated days.

analysis_steps.data_gaps: No carb tagging to separate meal-driven from correction-driven excursions; sparse loop-status sampling limits confirmation of dosing-potency swing frequency

analysis_steps.findings: Overnight glucose sits near target (90-107 mg/dL) with elevated TBR concentrated in local hours 0-1 (11.4% and 18.5%), more consistent with residual evening correction IOB than a standalone basal defect. A clear daytime rise occurs from local hour 8 through a peak at local hour 16 (average 162.8 mg/dL, 32.1% time above range), which coincides with the day's lowest basal segment (0.5 U/h at 16:00). A sharp evening decline follows (local hour 19 TBR 15.3%), overlapping plausible tail effects from afternoon corrections. Frequent 135 mg/dL Temporary Targets during parts of this window confound direct target-adequacy conclusions.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No basal-only (bolus-free) days isolated to separate basal effect from meal or correction effects; temp-target windows not cross-referenced at 5-minute resolution

analysis_steps.findings: Carb ratio segments cannot be assessed because zero carbohydrate entries exist anywhere in the package; this sub-area is blocked, not merely uncertain. The profile uses a single flat ISF value (56 mg/dL/U) for the entire day, while Dynamic ISF (70% adjustment factor) produces wide effective-sensitivity swings; this may reflect Dynamic ISF compensating for the lack of time-segmented ISF rather than a static ISF defect. DIA (10 hours) shows mixed fast (60-120 minute) and slow (240-360 minute) correction responses in therapy_response_windows, which is ambiguous as to whether 10 hours accurately reflects real insulin action or inflates tail IOB estimates. Target segments (90/100/90 mg/dL) appear plausible on their face but are confounded by frequent Temporary Target overrides.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No carbohydrate entries anywhere (blocks CR entirely); no isolated non-dynamic response data to separate static ISF adequacy from Dynamic ISF behavior

analysis_steps.findings: SMB and UAM are both enabled and function as the sole meal/rise-detection mechanism given zero carb logging, which is expected system behavior rather than a defect. smb_with_temp_target_enabled=true while smb_with_high_temp_target_enabled=false raises a material question about whether the repeated 135 mg/dL Temporary Targets are classified as high, which would suppress SMB delivery during those windows; evidence is mixed since one 180-minute 135 mg/dL window on 08-18 overlapped a poor-control day (TAR 15.3%) while a similar window on 08-17 overlapped a good day (TAR 4.2%), so this is a partial, unconfirmed contributor rather than a full explanation of the daytime pattern. SMB interval and duration limits (3/15/20 minutes) show no evidence of runaway or insufficient dosing frequency.

analysis_steps.data_gaps: AAPS's exact threshold for classifying a Temporary Target as high is not confirmed in the package; only two of several temp-target days were cross-checked against daily outcomes

analysis_steps.findings: Autosens disabled with Dynamic ISF enabled is an internally consistent configuration; sensitivity_ratio values of 1 correctly reflect neutral adjustment rather than a disabled mechanism. Max basal (12 U/h) and max IOB (25 U) both have large unused headroom relative to observed values (max enacted temp basal about 4 U/h, max observed IOB about 5.9 U), so neither ceiling is implicated in any observed episode. A non-inventory setting, current_basal_safety_multiplier (6.0), appears to be the operative cap during the severe 08-14 hyperglycemia event, where the algorithm requested about 5.9 U/h but was capped near 4 U/h; because this multiplier scales off the small scheduled basal segments, it structurally links back to basal segment sizing rather than being an independent automation defect. The carbohydrate absorption model (min_5m_carbimpact=8, meal_max_absorption_hours=7) is functionally untested since COB is always 0.

analysis_steps.findings: aaps_profile.analysis_context.meal_strategies is an empty array with no declared prebolus_minutes or immediate_bolus_percent, so no user-declared strategy exists to compare against telemetry; this is a genuine absence, not an omission. Telemetry confirms zero carbohydrate entries and zero meal-type boluses across the full period; treatment_summary and the sampled representative_treatments contain only Correction Bolus and Temp Basal events. Therapy_response_windows repeatedly show correction boluses followed by large glucose falls 120-360 minutes later (for example 2026-08-13, 08-14, 08-15, 08-16, 08-19, 08-20, 08-21), a pattern more consistent with reactive correction/IOB stacking against the 10-hour DIA than with a prebolus or CR sizing issue, though these cannot be fully separated from Dynamic ISF or basal effects.

No regular-carb-versus-e-carb comparison or duration/offset assessment is possible from this data.

analysis_steps.findings: The most consistent, cross-validated pattern across stages is the local-hour-16 glucose peak coinciding with the day's lowest basal segment (0.5 U/h), reinforced by an automation snapshot on 08-14 where the algorithm requested more basal than its safety-multiplier-derived ceiling allowed. This is prioritized as the primary, single, isolated review candidate. Delayed post-correction hypoglycemia (IOB stacking against 10-hour DIA) is a second, unresolved cross-cutting pattern that should be monitored rather than acted on simultaneously with any basal change. Dynamic ISF's wide swings plausibly compensate for a flat, non-time-segmented ISF profile and should not be changed until the basal review is evaluated in isolation. Carb ratio and e-carb settings remain fully blocked by the absence of any carbohydrate logging; the single highest-value next step to unblock future analysis is beginning approximate carb logging. All profile-period-applicability speculation from earlier checkpoints is now subordinated to the package's explicit historical_applicability declaration, with only residual uncertainty retained regarding the 08-13 Profile Switch event.

recommendations.title: Review the 16:00 basal segment against the recurring afternoon peak
recommendations.description: The local-hour-16 glucose peak (average 162.8 mg/dL, 32.1% time above range, the highest of any hour in the dataset) coincides with the day's lowest scheduled basal segment (0.5 U/h), and an automation snapshot on 08-14 shows requested basal exceeding its safety-multiplier ceiling during a severe hyperglycemia event tied to this window. Meal timing cannot be excluded as a contributor since no carbohydrate data exists, so this should be reviewed as an isolated, single change with close monitoring.

implementation_steps: Confirm with a care team or independently verify current profile settings and applicability before making any change, given the residual timeline uncertainty around the 2026-08-13 Profile Switch event
Make one isolated change at a time, starting with the 16:00 basal segment review, and monitor glucose closely for several days afterward before any further change
Do not change ISF, DIA, or Dynamic ISF settings at the same time as the basal change, since their effects would be confounded

Separately observe and document post-correction glucose trajectories through 6 hours over the next several corrections to evaluate the suspected IOB-stacking pattern before considering DIA or ISF changes

Clarify with AAPS documentation or a care team whether a 135 mg/dL temporary target is treated as a high temp target in the current build, to resolve the SMB suppression question
Reassess the full pattern set after two to three weeks of the above steps before considering any further profile or automation changes
education: Time-in-range, time-above-range, and time-below-range percentages describe the proportion of sensor readings within, above, and below a defined target range, and are commonly used alongside average glucose and coefficient of variation to summarize overall control

Insulin-on-board (IOB) stacking refers to the cumulative effect of multiple insulin doses whose action overlaps in time; a longer Duration of Insulin Action (DIA) setting extends the window in which this overlap can occur

Dynamic ISF adjusts the effective insulin sensitivity factor in real time based on recent glucose behavior, which can produce a wider range of effective sensitivity than a single flat profile ISF value would suggest on its own

Temporary Targets can change the effective glucose target for a defined duration and may also interact with certain automation settings, such as whether Super Micro Boluses (SMB) are permitted during a temporary target period
safety_notes: This is decision-support content only and does not constitute medical advice; TuneMyBG prepares data for review only
Any proposed change should be independently verified and discussed with a qualified care team before implementation
Changes should be made one at a time, never in combination with other dependent insulin-delivery settings, so that the effect of each change can be clearly observed
Glucose should be monitored closely after any change, with particular attention to hypoglycemia risk given the level-2 hypoglycemia clusters already observed in this data
The observed pattern of correction boluses followed by delayed glucose falls should be discussed with a care team before any additional insulin-dosing changes are made
